bipartite.kami_theme: The dawn mist over the Uji River, described as breaking apart into patches (tae-dae ni)
bipartite.shimo_theme: Through the thinning gaps in the mist, the wooden stakes of the fish-weirs (ajirogi) at Zeze become visible one after another
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku sets up a gradual atmospheric process — the morning mist over the Uji river breaking into disconnected patches — and the shimo-no-ku reveals what that dissolving mist uncovers to the eye: the ajirogi stakes emerging into view one by one along the river. The poem's entire effect depends on the temporal/visual pivot at 'tae-dae ni' (patchily/intermittently), which governs both the mist's fragmentation and the successive, piecemeal appearance of the stakes — the two are the same unfolding moment seen from cause (mist thinning) to effect (stakes appearing).

kigo.note: 川霧 (river mist) at dawn is a classical winter-season image in waka, especially associated with early winter mornings when mist rises off rivers in the cold air; combined with 朝ぼらけ (dawn) it evokes the crisp, cold stillness of a winter morning at Uji — a scene made famous in the Genji monogatari's Uji chapters. While 霧 can appear in autumn poetry as well, in the Hyakunin Isshu tradition this particular poem is classed as a winter poem (mikan/fuyu) owing to its explicit setting of early winter dawn over the river.
